set.summary: Egypt moved troops into Sinai from 15 May 1967, Nasser ordered the UN Emergency Force out on 18 May, and on 23 May Egypt closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. During the following 'waiting period' Foreign Minister Abba Eban sought Western diplomatic support, including a proposed international flotilla, while reservists were mobilised. On 1 June Moshe Dayan was appointed defence minister and opposition leader Menachem Begin joined a national unity government (the Knesset's record dates both ministers' terms from 5 June); on 4 June the cabinet authorised military action.

set.summary: During and after the war a large part of the population of the newly occupied areas left or was expelled; a UN report of October 1967 roughly estimated the number who fled at about 350,000. It counted about 200,000 people (about 93,000 of them UNRWA-registered refugees) who moved from the West Bank to the East Bank of Jordan and about 35,000 who crossed the Suez Canal from the Gaza Strip or Sinai; the Jewish Virtual Library gives about 325,000 Palestinians who fled the West Bank. From the Golan Heights (south-western Syria) about 110,000 people left according to Syrian sources and not more than 85,000 according to Israeli sources, including about 17,000 Palestinian refugees. In the Sinai town of East Kantara only 1,116 of about 15,000 inhabitants remained. Few were allowed to return.

set.summary: Israel launched pre-emptive air strikes on Egypt on 5 June 1967; Jordan and Syria entered the fighting, and by the ceasefire of 10 June Israel held the Sinai Peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. Israeli deaths are given as 776-983. Arab fatality estimates vary widely: roughly 10,000-15,000 Egyptian dead and missing; Jordanian losses from about 800 to about 6,000 (sources disagree); 1,000-2,500 Syrian; and about 2,000 Iraqi (a Jewish Virtual Library estimate). Israel now governed more than three-quarters of a million Palestinians in the occupied territories.

set.summary: Labour Minister (later Deputy Prime Minister) Yigal Allon proposed that Israel keep the Jordan Valley, East Jerusalem and the Etzion bloc while returning the densely populated West Bank hill areas to Jordan or to Palestinian self-rule. An initial version based on Palestinian autonomy was rejected by most ministers on 30 July 1967. The plan was never formally adopted, but at an April 1968 meeting of the Alignment's diplomatic committee most participants, except Moshe Dayan and Shimon Peres, backed it as the basis of policy. (On 19 June the cabinet had secretly decided to offer Sinai and the Golan for peace with Egypt and Syria.)

set.summary: Israeli forces raided the Fatah base at Karameh in the Jordan Valley in response to guerrilla attacks; Jordanian army units joined the fighting. Israeli dead are given as 28-33 and the Jordanian government's figure is 86 soldiers killed; by most accounts up to half of the several hundred Palestinian fighters were killed. Most of Karameh refugee camp was destroyed and 175 homes were razed. Israel withdrew the same day; Fatah presented the battle as a victory and recruitment to Palestinian guerrilla groups rose sharply.

set.summary: After years of restriction, emigration of Soviet Jews grew from 1969; about 149,000 Soviet Jews and their relatives came to Israel in 1970-1979 (Tolts), most of them in the early 1970s. From the mid-1970s a growing share of emigrants chose the United States instead: in 1976 about half (49%) went elsewhere, and by 1979 only one-third were arriving in Israel. Total immigration to Israel from all countries peaked at 55,888 in 1972.

set.summary: Artillery duels and raids along the Suez Canal, under way since 1967, escalated after Nasser declared a war of attrition in March 1969; Israel answered with commando raids and deep air strikes, and Soviet air-defence personnel deployed in Egypt. A US-brokered ceasefire took effect on 7-8 August 1970. Israel counts 1,424 soldiers and more than 100 civilians killed between 15 June 1967 and 8 August 1970; Egyptian deaths are estimated at about 5,000. The main cities on the Egyptian side of the canal were destroyed and about a million inhabitants were evacuated. Egyptian civilians were also killed: Israeli deep-penetration raids in early 1970 hit a factory at Abu Zaabal (89 workers killed) and a school at Bahr el-Baqar (30 children killed, per Egyptian reports; Israel said it had targeted military installations).

set.summary: Egypt and Syria launched a coordinated surprise attack on Yom Kippur, 6 October 1973, crossing the Suez Canal and advancing on the Golan. Israel stopped the Syrian advance, counter-attacked toward Damascus and crossed the canal; a US airlift resupplied Israel from mid-October. Fighting ended on 24-25 October after resolution 338. Israeli dead are given as about 2,520-2,800; Egyptian estimates range from about 5,000 to 15,000 and Syrian from 3,000 to 3,500; the Jewish Virtual Library also estimates losses of 125 Iraqi, 23 Jordanian, 100 Saudi and 200 Moroccan troops.

set.summary: Young Mizrahi Jews, mostly of Moroccan origin, from Jerusalem's Musrara neighbourhood formed the Black Panthers in early 1971 to protest poverty and discrimination; three days after their first demonstration the cabinet agreed to release extra funds for social programmes. Prime Minister Meir met them in April; the 'Night of the Panthers' rally on 18 May 1971 drew 5,000-7,000 people and ended in clashes with police, after which Meir called the Panthers 'not nice'.
